title: Erasable types and what survives at run time
hook: Almost everything TypeScript adds for typing is erased before JavaScript runs. Interfaces, type aliases, and most generics leave no trace in the output — unlike C# types that remain in Intermediate Language (IL) metadata for the Common Language Runtime (CLR) to enforce.

blocks.text: TypeScript follows an erasable types model: the compiler uses type information to report errors, then removes it during emit. What survives at run time is plain JavaScript — values, functions, classes (as constructors), and a few constructs that emit code (enums, decorators with experimental support, legacy namespace patterns). There is no parallel to CLR metadata tables listing your interfaces. Run-time type questions in JavaScript are answered with typeof, instanceof, Array.isArray, or custom validators — not with TypeScript interfaces.

entries.plainDefinition: Removing type annotations and type-only syntax so only JavaScript remains.
entries.example: interface User {} disappears; class User {} becomes a JavaScript function.

entries.plainDefinition: An import used only for types; guaranteed erased and not loaded at run time.
Compatibility is based on shape (properties), not declared names — and that shape is not stored at run time.
entries.example: Any object with { id: string } matches a User interface at compile time only.

blocks.text: Erasure explains why JSON.parse is never "safe" from TypeScript alone, why you cannot instanceof an interface, and why dependency injection containers in TS use decorators or manual registration unlike C# reflection. When an API returns unknown data, compile-time types lie unless you validate. Production services add Zod, io-ts, or JSON Schema at boundaries — the same place C# might use System.Text.Json with real DTO types plus optional validation attributes.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: TypeScript types are a compile-time fiction for the checker. JavaScript values at run time never carry interface tags. C# assemblies do carry type metadata the CLR reads.

items.title: Erased completely
items.body: interface, type alias, generic parameters, import type, satisfies (compile-time check only).

items.title: Emits JavaScript
items.body: class, function, const/let, enum (object or IIFE), namespace (legacy), decorators (when enabled).

items.title: Run-time checks you write
items.body: typeof, instanceof, in operator, custom type guards, schema validators.

items.title: C# contrast
items.body: Roslyn keeps type names in IL. CLR uses them for casting, reflection, serialization — no erasure.

diagram.title: Erasable types vs CLR metadata
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph ts [TypeScript]
    I[interface Order]
    C[class OrderService]
    I -->|erased| X[gone]
    C -->|emits| JS[function OrderService]
  end
  subgraph cs [C#]
    IC[interface IOrder]
    CL[class OrderService]
    IC --> META[IL metadata]
    CL --> META
    META --> CLR[CLR enforcement]
  end

snippet.label: Interfaces and types vanish
snippet.explanation: type and interface exist only for tsc. At run time order is any object JavaScript allows — wrong shapes throw at property access, not at a type boundary.

snippet.label: Classes emit — but generics erase
snippet.explanation: class becomes a constructor function. Generic <T> is compile-time only — unlike C# generic types that retain type args in metadata for reified generics on value types and reference types.

snippet.label: import type is fully erased
snippet.explanation: import type guarantees no run-time dependency on ./models.js. This is how you avoid circular bundle issues for type-only sharing.

snippet.label: Enums are a special case (they emit)
snippet.explanation: Enums break the pure erasure story — they generate JavaScript. Many codebases prefer const objects + union types to avoid enum emit quirks and bundler issues.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using as Order on JSON.parse without validation — the cast is a lie at run time. Expecting instanceof to work with interfaces. Assuming generic type parameters exist for reflection. Treating const enum as always inlined without checking isolatedModules.

blocks.text: TypeScript's design trades run-time type reification for zero overhead and full JavaScript interop. Branded/opaque types simulate nominal typing at compile time only. declare const enum with preserveConstEnums changes emit. experimentalDecorators + emitDecoratorMetadata (legacy) can emit design:type metadata for DI frameworks like NestJS — opt-in, not default. C# reflection can list properties on any object; TS needs libraries or code generation. For FAANG interviews: always mention unknown at API boundaries plus narrowing guards.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming TS types exist at run time. Using as casts on external data as 'validation'. Not knowing enums emit. Saying generics are reified like Java/C# without mentioning erasure.

interviewTakeaways: Interfaces, type aliases, and generic parameters erase — JavaScript engines never see them.
Classes and enums emit JavaScript; interfaces do not — instanceof works only on class constructors.
API boundaries need runtime validation (Zod, guards) because JSON.parse returns unknown shapes.
60s: TS types are compile-time only. Erased on emit. CLR keeps metadata. Use unknown + narrow at boundaries. Enums are the common exception that emits.
Follow-up: how would you model nominal IDs without run-time cost?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'TypeScript makes JSON.parse safe.' Strong: 'Only after schema parse or type guard — annotations erase.'
Trying instanceof MyInterface — interfaces do not exist at run time.
Strong answer: 'Erasure = zero runtime types. Validate at boundaries. C# keeps IL metadata; TS does not.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript run-time checks replace erased TypeScript types. typeof returns string tags; instanceof checks prototype chain.
Use unknown instead of any for external data, then narrow — compile-time safety without pretending types survive emit.
